claim: RNA polymerase (Pol) I is a 14-subunit enzyme that solely transcribes pre-ribosomal RNA.
source: RNA polymerase (Pol) I is a 14-subunit enzyme that solely transcribes pre-ribosomal RNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the composition and function of Pol I, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most of the nucleotide-bound ECs lack the A49-A34.5 heterodimer and adopt a Pol II-like conformation.
source: Strikingly, most of the nucleotide-bound ECs lack the A49-A34.5 heterodimer and adopt a Pol II-like conformation, in which the A12.2 C-terminal domain is bound in a previously unobserved position at the A135 surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structural data presented in the manuscript, specifically the observation that 63% of particles lacked the heterodimer.

claim: In the Pol I* EC, the A12.2 C-terminal domain is bound in a previously unobserved position at the A135 surface.
source: Strikingly, most of the nucleotide-bound ECs lack the A49-A34.5 heterodimer and adopt a Pol II-like conformation, in which the A12.2 C-terminal domain is bound in a previously unobserved position at the A135 surface.
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM structures showing A12.2C in a novel position, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reversible binding of the A49-A34.5 heterodimer could contribute to the regulation of Pol I transcription initiation and elongation.
source: Our structural and biochemical data suggest a mechanism where reversible binding of the A49-A34.5 heterodimer could contribute to the regulation of Pol I transcription initiation and elongation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural and biochemical data presented, including fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: All three eukaryotic RNA polymerases (Pol I, Pol II and Pol III) share a structurally conserved 10-subunit core and a 2-subunit stalk.
source: Although all three eukaryotic RNA polymerases (Pol I, Pol II and Pol III) share a structurally conserved 10-subunit core and a 2-subunit stalk, they have evolved distinct structural features, including accessory subunits, and rely each on a unique specialized set of general transcription factors (Engel et al., 2018; Khatter et al., 2017; Vannini and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Pol I relies on a simpler transcription initiation machinery compared to Pol II.
source: Accordingly, Pol I relies on a simpler transcription initiation machinery compared to Pol II (Keener et al., 1998), and similar to Pol III, has incorporated Pol II transcription factor-like subunits during evolution (Engel et al., 2018; Khatter et al., 2017; Vannini and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pol I has incorporated Pol II transcription factor-like subunits during evolution.
source: Accordingly, Pol I relies on a simpler transcription initiation machinery compared to Pol II (Keener et al., 1998), and similar to Pol III, has incorporated Pol II transcription factor-like subunits during evolution (Engel et al., 2018; Khatter et al., 2017; Vannini and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the first crystal structures, Pol I formed a dimer, thereby locking the enzyme in an inactive conformation.
source: In the first crystal structures, Pol I formed a dimer, thereby locking the enzyme in an inactive conformation (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous crystal structures.

claim: The Pol I DNA-binding cleft was very wide in the crystal structures.
source: Although the core structure was overall conserved compared to Pol II, the Pol I DNA-binding cleft was very wide, and it was occupied by the C-terminal domain of Pol I-specific subunit A12.2 and a DNA-mimicking loop/expander element that occupies the position of the DNA-RNA transcription bubble.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in previous crystal structures.

claim: The wide cleft conformation resulted in the unfolding of the bridge helix.
source: This wide cleft conformation resulted in the unfolding of the bridge helix, a conserved element that connects the two biggest subunits in multi-subunit RNA polymerases and plays an important role during catalysis (Weinzierl, 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from previous structural studies with a citation.

claim: Binding to a DNA-RNA scaffold promoted the closure of the DNA-binding cleft in Pol I.
source: Subsequent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Pol I elongation complex (EC) revealed that binding to a DNA-RNA scaffold promoted the closure of the DNA-binding cleft, thus freeing the active site for nucleotide binding and causing the folding of the bridge helix (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cryo-EM structures.

claim: The EC structures of Pol I were very similar to those observed for Pol II and Pol III.
source: The EC structures were very similar to those observed for Pol II (Kettenberger et al., 2004) and Pol III (Hoffmann et al., 2015), highlighting that the actively transcribing Pol I adopts a conserved conformation and suggesting that the enzymatic mechanism of nucleotide addition is functionally conserved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structures of Pol II and Pol III.

claim: The enzymatic mechanism of nucleotide addition is functionally conserved among Pol I, Pol II, and Pol III.
source: The EC structures were very similar to those observed for Pol II (Kettenberger et al., 2004) and Pol III (Hoffmann et al., 2015), highlighting that the actively transcribing Pol I adopts a conserved conformation and suggesting that the enzymatic mechanism of nucleotide addition is functionally conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity supported by citations.

claim: Mutating specific conserved residues in the Pol I and Pol II active sites appear to have different effects in vitro.
source: However, mutating specific conserved residues in the Pol I and Pol II active sites appear to have different effects in vitro (Viktorovskaya et al., 2013), suggesting that other elongation intermediates might reveal previously uncharacterized differences between Pol I and Pol II.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The basal Pol I initiation complex has a very different, much simpler architecture compared to Pol II.
source: Structural data of the basal Pol I initiation complex have revealed a very different, much simpler architecture compared to Pol II (Engel et al., 2017; Han et al., 2017; Sadian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The A49-A34.5 heterodimer has been proposed to function as both a TFIIF- and TFIIE-like factor.
source: In Pol I, the A49-A34.5 heterodimer (hereafter referred also as 'heterodimer') has been proposed to function as both, a TFIIF- and TFIIE-like factor, participating during transcription initiation and elongation (Geiger et al., 2010; Vannini and Cramer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The A49 C-terminal tandem winged helix domain (tWH) has structural homology to TFIIE.
source: While the A49 C-terminal tandem winged helix domain (tWH) has structural homology to TFIIE, the N-terminal A49 domain forms a dimer with the A34.5 subunit which adopts a triple β-barrel structure that resembles the Rap74/30 module of TFIIF (Geiger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: The N-terminal A49 domain forms a dimer with the A34.5 subunit which adopts a triple β-barrel structure that resembles the Rap74/30 module of TFIIF.
source: While the A49 C-terminal tandem winged helix domain (tWH) has structural homology to TFIIE, the N-terminal A49 domain forms a dimer with the A34.5 subunit which adopts a triple β-barrel structure that resembles the Rap74/30 module of TFIIF (Geiger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Deletion of either A49 or A34.5 results in a Pol I enzyme lacking both subunits.
source: However, as the dimerization domains contribute most to the binding, deletion of either subunit results in a Pol I enzyme lacking both subunits (Gadal et al., 1997; Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Pol I has been shown to exist in two different conformations that differ by the presence of the heterodimer, which can be reversibly dissociated.
source: Since its discovery, Pol I has been shown to exist in two different conformations that differ by the presence of the heterodimer, which can be reversibly dissociated (Huet et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The form lacking A49-A34.5, termed Pol I*, has reduced transcriptional specificity and activity compared to the complete Pol I enzyme.
source: The form lacking A49-A34.5, termed Pol I*, has reduced transcriptional specificity and activity compared to the complete Pol I enzyme (Huet et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The heterodimer appears to increase the processivity of Pol I.
source: Although the heterodimer appears to increase the processivity of Pol I, details of its function are still unknown.
evidence: This is a statement based on previous observations, though details remain unclear.

claim: Neither A49 nor A34.5 are essential genes.
source: Neither A49 (Liljelund et al., 1992) nor A34.5 (Gadal et al., 1997) are essential genes, and Pol I* has been proposed to co-exist with Pol I in vivo (Gadal et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Pol I* has been proposed to co-exist with Pol I in vivo.
source: Neither A49 (Liljelund et al., 1992) nor A34.5 (Gadal et al., 1997) are essential genes, and Pol I* has been proposed to co-exist with Pol I in vivo (Gadal et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deletion of topoisomerase I causes a very strong growth defect in yeast only when combined with a deletion of A34.5.
source: Deletion of topoisomerase I causes a very strong growth defect in yeast only when combined with a deletion of A34.5 (Gadal et al., 1997) suggesting that A34.5 is important for relieving topological stress during rDNA transcription.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: A34.5 is important for relieving topological stress during rDNA transcription.
source: Deletion of topoisomerase I causes a very strong growth defect in yeast only when combined with a deletion of A34.5 (Gadal et al., 1997) suggesting that A34.5 is important for relieving topological stress during rDNA transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic data cited from previous work.

claim: The A49-A34.5 heterodimer has a stronger effect on promoter-dependent transcription than on non-specific transcription in vitro.
source: In vitro, the A49-A34.5 heterodimer has a stronger effect on promoter-dependent transcription than on non-specific transcription, while addition of the A49 tWH domain is sufficient to restore promoter-dependent and non-specific transcription (Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Addition of the A49 tWH domain is sufficient to restore promoter-dependent and non-specific transcription.
source: In vitro, the A49-A34.5 heterodimer has a stronger effect on promoter-dependent transcription than on non-specific transcription, while addition of the A49 tWH domain is sufficient to restore promoter-dependent and non-specific transcription (Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous in vitro studies.

claim: A12.2 shares homology with Pol II subunit Rpb9 in its N-terminal domain and the Pol II cleavage factor TFIIS in its C-terminal domain.
source: The Pol I-specific subunit A12.2 also contains additional built-in functionality. A12.2 shares homology with Pol II subunit Rpb9 in its N-terminal domain and the Pol II cleavage factor TFIIS in its C-terminal domain (Ruan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The A12.2 C-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2C) is required for the Pol I intrinsic RNA cleavage activity.
source: The A12.2 C-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2C) is required for the Pol I intrinsic RNA cleavage activity (Kuhn et al., 2007) and adopts a similar position as TFIIS in the cleft in unbound (apo) Pol I (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013; Neyer et al., 2016) as well as in Pol I bound only to DNA (Sadian et al., 2017; Tafur et al., 2016), but is excluded from the active site upon formation of the EC (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental and structural studies.

claim: A12.2C adopts a similar position as TFIIS in the cleft in unbound (apo) Pol I.
source: The A12.2 C-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2C) is required for the Pol I intrinsic RNA cleavage activity (Kuhn et al., 2007) and adopts a similar position as TFIIS in the cleft in unbound (apo) Pol I (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013; Neyer et al., 2016) as well as in Pol I bound only to DNA (Sadian et al., 2017; Tafur et al., 2016), but is excluded from the active site upon formation of the EC (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: A12.2C is excluded from the active site upon formation of the EC.
source: The A12.2 C-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2C) is required for the Pol I intrinsic RNA cleavage activity (Kuhn et al., 2007) and adopts a similar position as TFIIS in the cleft in unbound (apo) Pol I (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013; Neyer et al., 2016) as well as in Pol I bound only to DNA (Sadian et al., 2017; Tafur et al., 2016), but is excluded from the active site upon formation of the EC (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Deletion of A12.2C does not cause any growth defect.
source: While deletion of A12.2C does not cause any growth defect, deletion of the A12.2 N-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2N) produces a similar effect as deletion of the complete protein (Van Mullem et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Deletion of the A12.2 N-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2N) produces a similar effect as deletion of the complete protein.
source: While deletion of A12.2C does not cause any growth defect, deletion of the A12.2 N-terminal Zn ribbon domain (A12.2N) produces a similar effect as deletion of the complete protein (Van Mullem et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Deletion of either the complete A12.2 or A12.2N alters the nucleolar localization of Pol I.
source: Interestingly, deletion of either the complete A12.2 or A12.2N also alters the nucleolar localization of Pol I, suggesting that A12.2 is important for Pol I integrity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous studies.

claim: A12.2 is important for Pol I integrity.
source: Interestingly, deletion of either the complete A12.2 or A12.2N also alters the nucleolar localization of Pol I, suggesting that A12.2 is important for Pol I integrity.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic data.

claim: The heterodimer stimulates A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage in vitro.
source: The heterodimer stimulates A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage in vitro (Geiger et al., 2010), the latter which is important for Pol I backtrack recovery (Lisica et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage is important for Pol I backtrack recovery.
source: The heterodimer stimulates A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage in vitro (Geiger et al., 2010), the latter which is important for Pol I backtrack recovery (Lisica et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A12.2N interacts directly with the dimerization domain of A49, thus stabilizing the anchoring of the heterodimer.
source: A12.2N interacts directly with the dimerization domain of A49, thus stabilizing the anchoring of the heterodimer (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: A12.2 has been proposed to be important for transcription initiation in vivo and in vitro, especially in the absence of A49.
source: Recently, A12.2 has also been proposed to be important for transcription initiation in vivo and in vitro, especially in the absence of A49 (Darrière et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: 63% of all particles selected after the first unmasked 3D classification step did not have the heterodimer bound and showed density for A12.2C in a new position.
source: In total, 63% of all particles selected after the first unmasked 3D classification step did not have the heterodimer bound and showed density for A12.2C in this new position (named Pol I* in analogy to RNA polymerase A* (Huet et al., 1975)), while only 37% represented the 14-subunit Pol I.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: 37% of particles represented the 14-subunit Pol I.
source: In total, 63% of all particles selected after the first unmasked 3D classification step did not have the heterodimer bound and showed density for A12.2C in this new position (named Pol I* in analogy to RNA polymerase A* (Huet et al., 1975)), while only 37% represented the 14-subunit Pol I.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The 12-subunit Pol I* EC lacking the heterodimer was refined to 3.18 Å resolution.
source: Extensive 3D classification ultimately yielded two different nucleotide-bound ECs: 12-subunit Pol I* EC lacking the heterodimer, which was refined to 3.18 Å resolution, and 14-subunit Pol I EC, which was refined to 3.42 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The 14-subunit Pol I EC was refined to 3.42 Å resolution.
source: Extensive 3D classification ultimately yielded two different nucleotide-bound ECs: 12-subunit Pol I* EC lacking the heterodimer, which was refined to 3.18 Å resolution, and 14-subunit Pol I EC, which was refined to 3.42 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The overall conformation of both Pol I forms is very similar, with the exception of the presence/absence of the heterodimer, the previously unobserved position of A12.2C and a slight difference in the conformation of the clamp.
source: The overall conformation of both Pol I forms is very similar, with the exception of the presence/absence of the heterodimer, the previously unobserved position of A12.2C and a slight difference in the conformation of the clamp, and resemble previously published structures (Figure 1) (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: An apo Pol I* reconstruction at 3.21 Å resolution was obtained with a similar conformation as previously observed for the cryo-EM structures of monomeric Pol I.
source: Interestingly, an apo Pol I* reconstruction at 3.21 Å resolution was also obtained with a similar conformation as previously observed for the cryo-EM structures of monomeric Pol I (Neyer et al., 2016; Pilsl et al., 2016), highlighting that the presence of the heterodimer and the novel position of A12.2C do not impose any conformational constraints on the Pol I core (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM structure determination with comparison to previous structures.

claim: The presence of the heterodimer and the novel position of A12.2C do not impose any conformational constraints on the Pol I core.
source: Interestingly, an apo Pol I* reconstruction at 3.21 Å resolution was also obtained with a similar conformation as previously observed for the cryo-EM structures of monomeric Pol I (Neyer et al., 2016; Pilsl et al., 2016), highlighting that the presence of the heterodimer and the novel position of A12.2C do not impose any conformational constraints on the Pol I core (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: In the 12-subunit Pol I* EC, lacking the heterodimer, the A12.2C occupies a novel position next to the A135 surface.
source: In the 12-subunit Pol I* EC, lacking the heterodimer, the A12.2C occupies a novel position next to the A135 surface (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The new position of A12.2C overlaps with the A34.5-Ct in the complete, 14-subunit Pol I EC.
source: This new position overlaps with the A34.5-Ct in the complete, 14-subunit Pol I EC (Figure 1B), where A12.2C is disordered and only density up to residue 67 is observed (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data with comparison to previous structures.

claim: In the 14-subunit Pol I EC, A12.2C is disordered and only density up to residue 67 is observed.
source: This new position overlaps with the A34.5-Ct in the complete, 14-subunit Pol I EC (Figure 1B), where A12.2C is disordered and only density up to residue 67 is observed (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data with citations to previous work.

claim: The new position of A12.2C resembles that of the C-terminal domain of Pol II subunit Rpb9, outside of the DNA-binding cleft.
source: The new position of A12.2C resembles that of the C-terminal domain of Pol II subunit Rpb9, outside of the DNA-binding cleft (Figure 1C, right), and is distinct from the previously reported TFIIS-like position near the active site (Figure 1C, left).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation.

claim: The A12.2C can move between TFIIS-like and Rpb9-like positions by rotating around a hinge located at residues 66–67.
source: The A12.2C can move between these positions by rotating around a hinge located at residues 66–67 (Figure 1A, Figure 1C, middle).
evidence: This is a structural observation and mechanistic interpretation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Binding to the TFIIS-like position is only possible when the DNA-binding cleft is open or partially open.
source: Whereas binding to the TFIIS-like position is only possible when the DNA-binding cleft is open (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013) or partially open (Neyer et al., 2016; Sadian et al., 2017; Tafur et al., 2016), binding to the Rpb9-like position can only occur when the heterodimer is absent.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations with citations.

claim: Binding to the Rpb9-like position can only occur when the heterodimer is absent.
source: Whereas binding to the TFIIS-like position is only possible when the DNA-binding cleft is open (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013) or partially open (Neyer et al., 2016; Sadian et al., 2017; Tafur et al., 2016), binding to the Rpb9-like position can only occur when the heterodimer is absent.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Different interactions occur in two areas of the A135 surface in Pol I* and Pol I.
source: Detailed analysis of Pol I* and Pol I reveals that different interactions occur in two areas of the A135 surface (Figure 2A, Figure 1C, middle).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The first area involves part of the A135 External Domain 1 (ED1), which interacts either with the A34.5-Ct (in Pol I) or A12.2C (in Pol I*).
source: The first area involves part of the A135 External Domain 1 (ED1), which interacts either with the A34.5-Ct (in Pol I) or A12.2C (in Pol I*).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The second area corresponds to part of the A135 Hybrid Binding (HB) domain (residues 989 to 1000), which in Pol I interacts with the A34.5-Ct but in Pol I* interacts with the A135 N-terminal tail (A135-Nt).
source: The second area corresponds to part of the A135 Hybrid Binding (HB) domain (residues 989 to 1000), which in Pol I interacts with the A34.5-Ct but in Pol I* interacts with the A135 N-terminal tail (A135-Nt), which folds back towards the HB domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The A135-Nt effectively acts as a switch, changing its positioning to allow or to prevent A34.5-Ct binding to the HB domain.
source: The A135-Nt effectively acts as a switch, changing its positioning to allow or to prevent A34.5-Ct binding to the HB domain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Both A12.2C and A34.5-Ct form similar interactions with the Pol I core, as both interact with two neighboring asparagine residues in the A135 ED1 (N683 and N684).
source: Both A12.2C and A34.5-Ct form similar interactions with the Pol I core, as both interact with two neighboring asparagine residues in the A135 ED1 (N683 and N684) (Figure 2B,C) and an aspartate residue (D990) in the A135 HB domain (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Both A12.2C and A34.5-Ct interact with an aspartate residue (D990) in the A135 HB domain.
source: Both A12.2C and A34.5-Ct form similar interactions with the Pol I core, as both interact with two neighboring asparagine residues in the A135 ED1 (N683 and N684) (Figure 2B,C) and an aspartate residue (D990) in the A135 HB domain (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: In the monomeric apo Pol I, A12.2C can still occupy the TFIIS-like position.
source: In the monomeric apo Pol I, A12.2C can still occupy the TFIIS-like position (Neyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: In the apo Pol I*, despite being sufficient space for accommodating A12.2C in the TFIIS-like position, A12.2C is observed in the Rpb9-like position.
source: However, in the apo Pol I*, despite being sufficient space for accommodating A12.2C in the TFIIS-like position, A12.2C is observed in the Rpb9-like position (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The presence of the heterodimer in the enzyme could promote binding of A12.2C to the TFIIS-like site (when accessible) by blocking the Rpb9-like binding site.
source: The presence of the heterodimer in the enzyme could thus promote binding of A12.2C to the TFIIS-like site (when accessible) by blocking the Rpb9-like binding site.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural observations.

claim: In apo Pol I*, the change in the position of A12.2C also shifts the A12.2N by ~3 Å towards the jaw.
source: In apo Pol I*, the change in the position of A12.2C also shifts the A12.2N by ~3 Å towards the jaw, and part of the latter appears to move towards the A12.2 linker, likely to stabilize its position (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Part of the jaw appears to move towards the A12.2 linker, likely to stabilize its position.
source: In apo Pol I*, the change in the position of A12.2C also shifts the A12.2N by ~3 Å towards the jaw, and part of the latter appears to move towards the A12.2 linker, likely to stabilize its position (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a structural observation with a mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Compared to the heterodimer alone, an increase in anisotropy was observed in a concentration-dependent manner as Pol I* EC was added.
source: Compared to the heterodimer alone, we observed an increase in anisotropy in a concentration-dependent manner as we added Pol I* EC (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The same experiment using wild type Pol I EC gave a right-shifted curve, indicating an exchange between endogenous heterodimer on wild type Pol I and labelled heterodimer.
source: The same experiment using wild type Pol I EC gave a right-shifted curve, indicating an exchange between endogenous heterodimer on wild type Pol I and labelled heterodimer.
evidence: This is a result from the fluorescence anisotropy experiments with interpretation.

claim: Heterodimer binding to Pol I is reversible.
source: These data suggest that heterodimer binding to Pol I is reversible, and that A12.2C binding A135 as observed in Pol I* does not irreversibly prevent heterodimer binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence anisotropy data.

claim: A12.2C binding A135 as observed in Pol I* does not irreversibly prevent heterodimer binding.
source: These data suggest that heterodimer binding to Pol I is reversible, and that A12.2C binding A135 as observed in Pol I* does not irreversibly prevent heterodimer binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence anisotropy data.

claim: Incubation of the Pol I*/A49-A34.5 sample with recombinant A12.2C (residues 79 to 125) for 30 min did not reduce the anisotropy even at 50-fold molar excess.
source: Incubation of the Pol I*/A49-A34.5 sample with recombinant A12.2C (residues 79 to 125) for 30 min did not reduce the anisotropy (indicating the release of the heterodimer from Pol I) even at 50-fold molar excess (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Incubation of the complex in the presence of GMPCPP did not change the anisotropy of the bound complex even at 20 mM.
source: Similarly, incubation of the complex in the presence of GMPCPP did not change the anisotropy of the bound complex even at 20 mM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Binding of the A12.2C to the Rpb9-like position is only possible after the heterodimer has dissociated from Pol I.
source: These results suggest that binding of the A12.2C to the Rpb9-like position is only possible after the heterodimer has dissociated from Pol I.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence anisotropy data.

claim: The Pol I ED1 diverges from its Pol II and Pol III counterparts, as it is smaller and lacks an extension that overlaps with A12.2C in the Rpb9-like position.
source: Comparison of Pol I* with Pol II and Pol III reveals that while the External Domain 2 (ED2) appears to be structurally more conserved, the Pol I ED1 diverges from its Pol II and Pol III counterparts, as it is smaller and lacks an extension that overlaps with A12.2C in the Rpb9-like position (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation.

claim: In Pol II, the Rpb9 C-terminal domain (Rpb9C) also binds the ED1, although differently than A12.2C due to the presence of an extension in the ED1.
source: In Pol II, the Rpb9 C-terminal domain (Rpb9C) also binds the ED1, although differently than A12.2C due to the presence of an extension in the ED1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation with citation.

claim: The Pol I and Pol II ED1 are specifically tailored to bind A12.2C and Rpb9C, respectively.
source: Therefore, the Pol I and Pol II ED1 are specifically tailored to bind A12.2C and Rpb9C, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative structural analysis.

claim: In Pol III, binding of the C11 C-terminal domain (C11C) in an Rbp9C-like position is precluded by the presence of a helix from subunit C53.
source: The Pol III ED1, as in Pol II, also has an extension in a region that overlaps with the position of A12.2C, but in addition, binding of the C11 C-terminal domain (C11C, equivalent to Pol I A12.2C and Pol II Rbp9C) in an Rbp9C-like position is precluded by the presence of a helix from subunit C53.
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation with citation.

claim: The C11C adopts a position far from the Pol III ED1 that differs from the position of both A12.2C and Rpb9C.
source: Accordingly, the C11C adopts a position far from the Pol III ED1 (Hoffmann et al., 2015) that differs from the position of both A12.2C and Rpb9C (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation with citation.

claim: No differences were observed between the active sites of Pol I* and 14-subunit Pol I.
source: Because the Pol I* EC reconstruction was obtained in the presence of the non-hydrolysable nucleotide analog GMPCPP and 1 mM MgCl2, we carefully compared the Pol I* active site with the active site in the 14-subunit Pol I reconstruction. As no differences were observed between the active sites, we pooled particles from both EC reconstructions, and classified them by restricting the classification to the core enzyme and the DNA-RNA hybrid using a soft mask and higher weight on the data (Scheres, 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from the cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The NTP is positioned in the 'A' site, as previously seen in Pol II and bacterial RNA polymerase.
source: As suggested by the conservation of residues in this region, the NTP is positioned in the 'A' site, as previously seen in Pol II (Cheung et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2006; Westover et al., 2004) and bacterial RNA polymerase (bcPol) (Vassylyev et al., 2007) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a structural observation with citations to previous work.

claim: The phosphate moiety of GMPCPP is bound by two invariant arginine residues (A135 R714 and R957).
source: Accordingly, the phosphate moiety is bound by two invariant arginine residues (A135 R714 and R957).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The conserved A190 N625 and R591, which are involved in NTP/dNTP discrimination, come close to the 3'- and 2'-OH group, respectively.
source: In addition, the conserved A190 N625 and R591, which are involved in NTP/dNTP discrimination, come close to the 3'- and 2'-OH group, respectively.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The NTP is maintained in the correct position by L1202 from the trigger loop, which interacts with the guanosine base.
source: The NTP is maintained in the correct position by L1202 from the trigger loop, which interacts with the guanosine base.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The positioning of the NTP substrate in the Pol I active site is virtually identical to that in Pol II.
source: Overall, the positioning of the NTP substrate in the Pol I active site is virtually identical to that in Pol II (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation.

claim: In both the Pol I and Pol I* EC, the downstream edge of the transcription bubble is stabilized by interactions of Pol I with nucleotides +1 and +2 from the NT strand.
source: An interesting scenario is also observed opposite to the NTP binding site, where Pol I displays features similar to Pol II and bcPol. In both, the Pol I and Pol I* EC, the downstream edge of the transcription bubble is stabilized by interactions of Pol I with nucleotides + 1 and+2 from the NT strand.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The +2 base is flipped into a pocket formed by elements from the A135 subunit, namely, the fork loop 2 (FL2) and loop B.
source: The +2 base is flipped into a pocket formed by elements from the A135 subunit, namely, the fork loop 2 (FL2) and loop B (Tafur et al., 2016) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data with citation.

claim: The A135 pocket resembles the β-pocket formed by the β subunit in bcPol.
source: These two elements form a pocket ('A135 pocket') which resembles that formed by the β subunit ('β-pocket') in bcPol (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation with citation.

claim: A phenylalanine from the A135 FL2 (F508) appears to stack with the +1 base, in an analogous fashion as W183 from the bcPol β subunit.
source: Whereas loop B exposes several positively charged residues towards the cavity of the A135 pocket that likely stabilize the phosphate backbone, a phenylalanine from the A135 FL2 (F508) appears to stack with the +1 base, in an analogous fashion as W183 from the bcPol β subunit (Zhang et al., 2012) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data with citation.

claim: The highly conserved D395 interacts with the +2 base as in bcPol and Pol II.
source: Finally, the highly conserved D395 also interacts with the +2 base as in bcPol (β subunit D446) (Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) and Pol II (Rpb2 D399) (Cheung and Cramer, 2011), and probably also in Pol III (C128 D370).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data with citations.

claim: Neither Pol II nor Pol III can form the equivalent interactions as in the A135 pocket because their corresponding loop B is differently positioned and far from the +1 and +2 bases.
source: However, neither Pol II nor Pol III can form the equivalent interactions as in the A135 pocket because their corresponding loop B is differently positioned and far from the +1 and+2 bases.
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation.

claim: Both sets of interactions are formed only when the DNA-binding cleft is completely closed and the jaw and clamp modules move towards each other.
source: Interestingly, both sets of interactions are formed only when the DNA-binding cleft is completely closed and the jaw and clamp modules move towards each other (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Formation of the EC involves the coarse movement of modules 1 and 2.
source: Thus, while formation of the EC involves the coarse movement of modules 1 and 2, nucleotide stabilization in the active site requires a more subtle, modular rearrangement.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Nucleotide stabilization in the active site requires a more subtle, modular rearrangement.
source: Thus, while formation of the EC involves the coarse movement of modules 1 and 2, nucleotide stabilization in the active site requires a more subtle, modular rearrangement.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: A12.2C can alternate between TFIIS-like and Rpb9-like positions depending on the presence of the A49-A34.5 heterodimer.
source: Here, we show that A12.2C can alternate between TFIIS-like and Rpb9-like positions depending on the presence of the A49-A34.5 heterodimer.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: In the TFIIS-like position, A12.2C is positioned in the DNA-binding cleft and occludes the active site, which is incompatible with NTP incorporation but in accordance with RNA cleavage.
source: In the TFIIS-like position, A12.2C is positioned in the DNA-binding cleft and occludes the active site, which is incompatible with NTP incorporation but in accordance with RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: When the cleft closes, A12.2C is excluded from the active site and can bind to the A135 ED1.
source: When the cleft closes (and thereby clashes with A12.2C in the TFIIS-like position), A12.2C is excluded from the active site and can bind to the A135 ED1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Binding of A12.2C and heterodimer to the ED1 are mutually exclusive, as A12.2C and A34.5-Ct use overlapping binding sites.
source: Binding of A12.2C and heterodimer to the ED1 are mutually exclusive, as A12.2C and A34.5-Ct use overlapping binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Exclusion of the heterodimer in this conformation is supported by the movement of the A135-Nt towards the HB domain, which blocks the interaction of the distal part of the A34.5-Ct with this domain.
source: Exclusion of the heterodimer in this conformation is supported by the movement of the A135-Nt towards the HB domain, which blocks the interaction of the distal part of the A34.5-Ct with this domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: The surface of A135 (in particular, the ED1) plays a pivotal role in specific factor exchange in Pol I.
source: These results suggest a mechanism by which the surface of A135 (in particular, the ED1) plays a pivotal role in specific factor exchange in Pol I.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural data.

claim: A12.2 may be involved in modulation of the movement of the jaw/lobe interface especially in the absence of A49.
source: Recent genetic studies have suggested that A12.2 may be involved in modulation of the movement of the jaw/lobe interface especially in the absence of A49, as the A49 linker and tWH domain appear to stabilize the closed conformation of Pol I when bound to DNA (Darrière et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent genetic studies.

claim: The A49 linker and tWH domain appear to stabilize the closed conformation of Pol I when bound to DNA.
source: Recent genetic studies have suggested that A12.2 may be involved in modulation of the movement of the jaw/lobe interface especially in the absence of A49, as the A49 linker and tWH domain appear to stabilize the closed conformation of Pol I when bound to DNA (Darrière et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent genetic studies.

claim: The A12.2C might restrict the movement of the lobe.
source: As the A12.2C binds to the A135 ED1, which sits next to the A135 lobe, the A12.2C might restrict the movement of the lobe.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Both A12.2 domains could regulate cleft opening/closing of Pol I upon DNA binding, as well as binding to the +1 and +2 nucleotides in the non-template strand.
source: Thus, while A12.2N regulates the flexibility of the jaw, A12.2C could additionally regulate the movement of the lobe. Together, both A12.2 domains could therefore regulate cleft opening/closing of Pol I upon DNA binding, as well as binding to the +1 and+2 nucleotides in the non-template strand (see above).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Restriction of movement of the A135 lobe by A12.2C might be important to maintain the closed state in the absence of A49.
source: Restriction of movement of the A135 lobe by A12.2C might be important to maintain the closed state in the absence of A49, as in Pol I*.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations.

claim: When the heterodimer is present in the complex, A12.2 might destabilize the EC as it can only occupy the TFIIS-like site, thereby preventing cleft closure.
source: In contrast, when the heterodimer is present in the complex, A12.2 might destabilize the EC as it can only occupy the TFIIS-like site, thereby preventing cleft closure (Appling et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation with citation.

claim: A49 could play an important role in maintaining a narrow cleft, which would also explain the stimulatory role of the heterodimer on A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage.
source: In this scenario, A49 could play an important role in maintaining a narrow cleft, which would also explain (in addition to the direct interaction of their N-terminal domains with A12.2) the stimulatory role of the heterodimer on A12.2-mediated RNA cleavage (Geiger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation with citation.

claim: Heterodimer association to Pol I might offer an additional layer of regulation of rDNA transcription in vivo.
source: In vivo, heterodimer association to Pol I might offer an additional layer of regulation of rDNA transcription (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The proportion of initiation-competent Pol I molecules in the cell has been proposed to represent those Pol I particles bound to initiation factor Rrn3.
source: The proportion of initiation-competent Pol I molecules in the cell has been proposed to represent those Pol I particles bound to initiation factor Rrn3 (Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The number of Pol I* particles in the cell could represent a population of actively transcribing DNA-bound Pol I, but also a pool of pre-active Pol I that can readily initiate transcription upon heterodimer binding and Rrn3 recruitment.
source: In contrast, the number of Pol I* particles in the cell could represent a population of actively transcribing DNA-bound Pol I, but also a pool of pre-active Pol I that can readily initiate transcription upon heterodimer binding and Rrn3 recruitment (in contrast to Pol I dimers, which appear to be a storage form of the enzyme (Torreira et al., 2017)).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation with citation.

claim: The number of initiation-competent Pol I molecules could be regulated not only by Pol I homo-dimerization and association with Rrn3, but also by changes in the heterodimer concentration in the nucleolus.
source: The number of initiation-competent Pol I molecules could be thus regulated not only by Pol I homo-dimerization and association with Rrn3, but also by changes in the heterodimer concentration in the nucleolus, thereby controlling the ratio of Pol I to Pol I*.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Nutrient-dependent regulation of nucleolar localization of the mammalian A49-A34.5 homolog PAF53-PAF49 has been observed.
source: Nutrient-dependent regulation of nucleolar localization of the mammalian A49-A34.5 homolog PAF53-PAF49 has been observed (Penrod et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PAF49 (A34.5 counterpart) accumulates in the nucleolus in growing cells but disperses to the nucleoplasm upon serum starvation.
source: PAF49 (A34.5 counterpart) accumulates in the nucleolus in growing cells but disperses to the nucleoplasm upon serum starvation (Yamamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In yeast, A34.5 is maintained in the nucleolus by its association with A49.
source: In yeast, A34.5 is maintained in the nucleolus by its association with A49 (but also contains a nucleolar localization signal in its C-terminal region), and A49 is required for the high loading rate of Pol I onto rDNA (Albert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A49 is required for the high loading rate of Pol I onto rDNA.
source: In yeast, A34.5 is maintained in the nucleolus by its association with A49 (but also contains a nucleolar localization signal in its C-terminal region), and A49 is required for the high loading rate of Pol I onto rDNA (Albert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Human PAF53-PAF49 can substitute the A49-A34.5 heterodimer in vivo suggesting a conserved function.
source: Human PAF53-PAF49 can substitute the A49-A34.5 heterodimer in vivo (Albert et al., 2011) suggesting a conserved function (and possibly regulation).
evidence: This is supported by a citation with inference about conservation.

claim: Regulation of heterodimer binding to Pol I might explain why promoter association of Pol I-Rrn3 complexes is low upon nutrient starvation even when the concentration of such complexes is relatively high.
source: Regulation of heterodimer binding to Pol I might also explain why promoter association of Pol I-Rrn3 complexes is low upon nutrient starvation even when the concentration of such complexes is relatively high (Torreira et al., 2017); the levels of the heterodimer might further regulate Pol I initiation rates.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation with citation.

claim: The levels of the heterodimer might further regulate Pol I initiation rates.
source: Regulation of heterodimer binding to Pol I might also explain why promoter association of Pol I-Rrn3 complexes is low upon nutrient starvation even when the concentration of such complexes is relatively high (Torreira et al., 2017); the levels of the heterodimer might further regulate Pol I initiation rates.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Release of the heterodimer from the enzyme would allow the binding of elongation factors to Pol I.
source: In addition, the release of the heterodimer from the enzyme would also allow the binding of elongation factors to Pol I.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural observations.

claim: Pol I has been shown to bind to elongation factor Spt5 directly.
source: Pol I has been shown to bind to elongation factor Spt5 directly (Viktorovskaya et al., 2011) and its activity is affected by Spt4/5 in vivo (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pol I activity is affected by Spt4/5 in vivo.
source: Pol I has been shown to bind to elongation factor Spt5 directly (Viktorovskaya et al., 2011) and its activity is affected by Spt4/5 in vivo (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the Pol I EC, canonical binding of Spt4/5 is precluded by the A49 tWH.
source: In the Pol I EC, canonical binding of Spt4/5 (as in the Pol II EC) is precluded by the A49 tWH (Tafur et al., 2016), as it occupies a position equivalent to the KOW1-L1 domain of Spt5, and by the A49 linker helix spanning the cleft, which clashes with the N-terminal region of Spt5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Bernecky et al., 2017; Ehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a structural observation with citations.

claim: Spt5 interacts physically and genetically with A49, suggesting a functional interplay between these proteins.
source: Interestingly, Spt5 interacts physically and genetically with A49, suggesting a functional interplay between these proteins (Viktorovskaya et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Paf1C has been shown to stimulate Pol I transcription in vivo and in vitro.
source: Paf1C, another elongation factor, has also been shown to stimulate Pol I transcription in vivo and in vitro (Zhang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Paf1C binds to Pol II on the outer surface of subunit Rpb2 including the Rpb2 ED2 and lobe.
source: Paf1C binds to Pol II on the outer surface of subunit Rpb2 (Pol II counterpart of A135) including the Rpb2 ED2 and lobe (Vos et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work.

claim: Paf1C clashes and competes with TFIIF for Pol II binding.
source: In this position, it clashes and competes with TFIIF for Pol II binding (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Heterodimer dissociation from Pol I could potentially free the binding site for both Spt4/5 and Paf1C.
source: Heterodimer dissociation from Pol I could potentially free the binding site for both Spt4/5 and Paf1C in a mechanism that could be akin to the transition from initiation to elongation in Pol II: while TFIIE (A49 tWH) blocks the Spt4/5 binding site, TFIIF (A49-A34.5 dimerization domain) occupies the binding site of part of Paf1C (Vos et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations and citations.

claim: Binding of elongation factors is mutually exclusive with the presence of initiation factors.
source: Thus, binding of elongation factors is mutually exclusive with the presence of initiation factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: In Pol I, factor exchange during the transition from initiation to elongation could be accommodated more readily just by the release of the heterodimer and switching to the Pol I* form.
source: Therefore, in Pol I, factor exchange during the transition from initiation to elongation could be accommodated more readily just by the release of the heterodimer and switching to the Pol I* form.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural observations.

claim: A12.2 might prevent re-association of the heterodimer.
source: In this scenario, A12.2 might further prevent re-association of the heterodimer.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation.

claim: A similar allosteric transition during promoter escape mediated by the heterodimer, Spt5 and the stalk has been previously proposed for Pol I.
source: A similar allosteric transition during promoter escape mediated by the heterodimer, Spt5 and the stalk has been previously proposed for Pol I (Beckouët et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Release of the heterodimer in vivo might be directly induced by Spt4/5 and Paf1C.
source: Because we could not observe any effect of free A12.2C on heterodimer binding to Pol I in vitro, release of the heterodimer in vivo might be directly induced by Spt4/5 and Paf1C.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the biochemical data.
